reflections.reflection: Linda told me the truth. Not in so many words — she is a professional and I am her subordinate and there are things neither of us can say directly — but she told me the truth. She confirmed the personal auto book is terminal. She said her pivot memo to corporate has gone unanswered. She asked me about my own timeline. That is not a manager asking an idle question. That is someone who respects me enough to hand me the signal without spelling it out. I have been living in bargaining — telling myself that if I learned SQL fast enough, if I gave Linda good enough data, if the pivot memo landed right, there would be a seat at the new table with my name on it. Maybe there still is. But I have to stop organizing my decisions around that hope as if it were a fact. I know what the policy numbers say. I built the query. I ran the aggregation. The slope does not bend back. I am 29, I have skills that transfer, I have no dependents, and I have roughly eight or nine months of runway before this becomes an emergency. That is not a crisis. That is an asset — if I use it deliberately.
reflections.identity_shift: The identity I have been carrying — 'I'm not scared of change' — has been partly performance. I said it, I believed it in the abstract, but I kept deferring the concrete actions that would prove it. The SQL course habit is real now. Three modules done, a working query built, a professional outreach to David Chen drafted and sent. That is not narrating a character. That is living one. The shift I feel this tick is not from comfortable to scared — it is from adaptive in self-description to adaptive in behavior. Those are different things and it took six ticks to close the gap.
regrets: I did not start a quiet job market scan earlier. I had the information by tick 4. I spent tick 5 on a module instead of also looking at the landscape. Both were worth doing. I only did one.

I have not yet formally registered for the $2,500 retraining grant. Maria Santos's office put money on a table and I keep noting it and not picking it up. That is a specific failure of follow-through that I cannot explain away with busyness.
successes: Module 3 complete. Not just finished — I built an actual output. A working query on hypothetical commercial fleet incident data. That is a portfolio artifact, not just a checkbox.

The Linda one-on-one worked. I gave honest field intelligence, I did not soften it, and she responded by treating me like an adult rather than a number. That is exactly what I wanted from that conversation.

The David Chen outreach is drafted and sent. Peer-to-peer, no desperation signal, real data to offer. It cost me thirty minutes and positions me in a sector-adjacent network I did not have six ticks ago.
reflections.adaptation_notes: Next two ticks are decision ticks, not preparation ticks. The preparation phase has been productive and necessary — but I am approaching the window where preparation without movement becomes avoidance wearing a productive mask. By tick 8 or 9 I should have: (1) the grant application submitted, (2) at least one informational interview in the data or insurtech space, (3) a clear read on whether Linda has heard back from corporate on the pivot memo. If she has not heard back by tick 8, I begin treating my departure as likely rather than possible. I do not catastrophize. I do not freeze. I move.

reflections.reflection: I am officially unemployed. The employment_status flipped in tick 8 — whether it was the honest signal I gave Linda, or the structural reality of what the office had become, or both at once, the outcome is the same: zero income, $10,640 in savings, $3,341 in monthly expenses, and 3.2 months of runway before this becomes an emergency. Tom Bradley got laid off. I did not. Linda protected the person who was building transferable skills and giving honest intelligence. That is information about her character and it is information about what mattered in this situation. I want to hold onto that clearly, not as comfort but as a data point about what professional integrity produces in practice. The inbox this tick showed me Linda still fighting: a second memo to corporate with a 14-day deadline, CRMP certification work she is treating as a live portfolio. She is not giving up on the pivot. She is also not giving up on herself. I respect that. It does not change my situation. I need income in a window that is narrowing. Two applications are out. No responses yet — normal, it is early — but waiting passively is not how I close the gap between runway and offer letter. The job search is now my full-time job. Module 4 is in progress. I am three-quarters through a certification that is currently the clearest differentiator I have. I finish it. I also reached out to Tom because it was the right thing to do and because I am not the kind of person who lets a colleague disappear into a difficult moment without saying something.
reflections.identity_shift: At tick 6 I noted the shift from adaptive in self-description to adaptive in behavior. Now I am testing whether that shift holds under actual financial pressure. The narrative I carry — 'I am not scared of change' — is no longer an abstract claim. It is being tested in real time against a shrinking bank account and a contracting sector and a 67% employment rate in the broader community. What I notice is that I am not frozen. I am not catastrophizing. I am making the next move. That is not heroism — it is just not collapsing. But not collapsing when the situation is genuinely hard is different from saying you will not collapse when things were still okay. The identity is being tested now. So far it is holding.
regrets: I still never applied for the $2,500 retraining grant from Maria Santos's office. I mentioned it in my tick 6 reflection as a specific failure of follow-through. I did not correct it in ticks 7 or 8. I am unemployed now and I am still not sure I applied. That is two and a half thousand dollars I may have left on the table during a period when I had runway to spare. I cannot undo that. I can apply now, immediately, this tick, and stop narrating the oversight.

The job search opening in tick 8 was the right move but it should have been tick 6 or 7. I let preparation be the comfortable substitute for the uncomfortable act of actually submitting applications. I knew this. I wrote it in my tick 6 reflection. I did it anyway. The pattern of insight followed by deferred action has cost me runway.
successes: I told Linda the truth at tick 8 and she did not retaliate. She protected me when the staffing cut came. The honesty was the right move both ethically and strategically. I want to note this clearly: professional honesty produced a professional outcome. That matters for how I navigate the next job.

Two applications are out. They are real applications, not informational conversations, not networking coffees dressed up as applications. The portfolio artifact — the fleet incident data query — is attached. I am a real candidate with a real artifact and two real companies have my materials.

Module 4 started. The course discipline has been the most consistent behavior I have maintained since tick 0. I have not missed a module since I started taking them seriously. That consistency is worth more than any single module.
reflections.adaptation_notes: The next three ticks determine whether I navigate this transition on my terms or on the market's terms. Follow-up on existing applications is now as important as submitting new ones. Three applications in flight by end of tick 9 is the minimum. If no response by tick 11, I expand geographic scope or consider adjacent roles I have been deprioritizing. I also need to apply for the retraining grant this tick — no more noting it and deferring it. Runway math: at $3,341/month burn and $10,640 savings, I have approximately 3.2 months before zero. If I land a role by tick 12, I am fine. If not, I need to consider reducing expenses or generating bridge income. I am not there yet. But I need to have the bridge income scenario mapped before I need it, not after.
